core.p: **Part (b)**: Explain the importance of Christmas **elsewhere in the novella**. In your answer you must consider: how Christmas is presented; why Christmas is important to Dickens’s message. You should refer to the context. (20 marks)

plan: Fezziwig and the Cratchits: generosity and family
essays.q: Explain the importance of Christmas elsewhere in the novella.
essays.t: Model essay: family, generosity and Christmas
essays.text:
Dickens presents Christmas not just as a festival but as a moral standard, a season of family, generosity and fellowship against which every character is judged, and he uses it to urge his readers to live by these values ‘all the year’.

The novella opens with two opposing definitions. Scrooge dismisses the season with ‘Bah! Humbug!’ and comically wishes that anyone saying ‘Merry Christmas’ could be ‘boiled with his own pudding’. Fred, ‘all in a glow’, answers with a speech that sums up Dickens’s values: Christmas is ‘a kind, forgiving, charitable, pleasant time’ when people treat those ‘below them’ as ‘fellow-passengers to the grave’. The metaphor stresses equality in death and so the duty of the rich to the poor. Writing in 1843, as Christmas was being revived as a family festival, Dickens deliberately attaches a social conscience to it.

Christmas is then shown through generosity and family. In Stave 2, Fezziwig’s Christmas ball includes everyone from apprentices to the housemaid, and Scrooge admits that his employer’s happiness was ‘quite as great as if it cost a fortune’: generosity is about spirit, not money. In Stave 3 the Cratchits, who are poor, celebrate with complete joy; Mrs Cratchit is ‘brave in ribbons’ and the family greets the pudding with delight. Their warmth contrasts with Scrooge’s ‘one coal’ in Stave 1, showing that Christmas wealth is measured in love.

The Ghost of Christmas Present extends Christmas beyond the family. He shows miners, lighthouse keepers and sailors keeping the festival in harsh conditions, and he sprinkles blessings on the poor people’s dinners. Yet he also reveals Ignorance and Want, reminding readers that Christmas joy must include the neglected. Dickens uses the season of plenty to sharpen the contrast with poverty.

In Stave 5, Scrooge proves that he has learned to keep Christmas. He sends the turkey to the Cratchits, gives to the charity collector, and is welcomed at Fred’s ‘Wonderful party’. His vow to ‘honour Christmas in my heart, and try to keep it all the year’ shows that Christmas values must outlast the day itself, and the narrator’s final judgement, that ‘he knew how to keep Christmas well’, sets the standard for the reader. By calling his chapters ‘staves’, as in a carol, Dickens presents the whole book as a song of Christmas to be shared, so that its values can spread from home to home.
essays.thesis: Dickens presents Christmas not just as a festival but as a moral standard, a season of family, generosity and fellowship against which every character is judged, and he uses it to urge his readers to live by these values ‘all the year’.
why: **AO1**: an argument (Christmas as a moral standard) sustained across the text.
**AO3**: Christmas revival 1843, staves as carol, poverty.

summary: A full grade 9 part (b) model essay on family, generosity and Christmas, arguing that Dickens presents Christmas as a moral standard of connection and generosity that Scrooge must learn to keep all year.
